He steps into the shallow, wide creek, parts the reeds, and wades toward the far bank. Behind him, the campfire flickers along with the singing beneath the clear night sky. The lad in the company whose forebears had served as Catastrophe Messengers swore on his mother's honor that nothing would go wrong for a week, and so 'Shchin' made camp here. The soldiers sit clustered in twos and threes now; only one newcomer, transferred from the vanguard company not long ago, has crossed the water alone, on some errand no one can guess.
As their leader, Styopa has a duty to know, and so he follows the trail those military boots have left. The faint marks of a footprint several sizes smaller than his own, pressed into the mud, lead him to a small Originium lamp.
Styopa sits himself down on the ground without waiting to be asked. Those eyes have been fixed on him since the moment he appeared.
'Nervous? About tomorrow's fight.'
'No. They're only mountain bandits.'
'You say that, but this is still the first operation you've had since joining us. I understand. By the way—can you actually sing, or not?'
The gaze that had merely been direct turns inexplicably fierce in an instant. Styopa scratches his head. He had meant to apologize for the way the others heckled her earlier, but by the time the words reach his lips they very nearly become a repeat of the standoff from before.
'Can't, it seems. But that's fine—I can't either. Next time those louts ask you to sing, do what I do and simply recite the words.
'One of our old grandmothers set a house of glass upon a fowlbeast's two legs.
'Not so that it might migrate as we do, but so that it might turn to face any way, at any moment—'
Song cuts off Styopa's 'demonstration.' After a few lines, the voice grows fainter. She stops.
'So you can sing.' Styopa laughs, untroubled by whether he has read the matter wrong. 'If you simply don't want to, you can just say so. We aren't like the other regulars—we don't stand on that many taboos.'
'I'll get used to it.'
With a click, the Originium lamp goes out. In the dark, the light of Arts leaps from the tip of the Freeman's blade like a single eye. The blade's owner rises and gestures for the soldier to follow him.

The leader's tent is unexpectedly tidy; only a coat lies spread out on the camp bed. An assortment of weapons is laid out across the thick fabric, and beside them a towel worn grey with use and a basin of water show that their owner is in the middle of cleaning his gear.
'Give me a moment.' Styopa walks over and lifts the coat, rummaging through its countless pockets, and after a long while finally fishes out an oval piece of iron.
'I should have had it finished sooner. I kept getting caught up planning routes and never finished the engraving. It's about done now. Here.'
The grey-haired youth runs her fingers over the raised letters on the iron and says nothing.
"'Irina Elianovna'... I don't think I got the name wrong. Oh, and take this too. There's a spell of mine left on it."
A silver dagger appears from somewhere unknown.
'So long as you don't lose it, and so long as I'm still alive, the Arts set upon it will shield you from one lethal blow. Everyone here has one.
'It's a little late to be saying it, but—welcome to Shchin.'
The soldier nods and takes the dagger. She looks at the iron tag in her hand, then at the chain around Styopa's neck, hung heavy with dog tags of every make, and her voice is as flat as ever.
'Thank you.
'Though in truth, ending up like that would be fine too. For a soldier, it isn't a bad way to finish.'
